$comment: Shared table for the XML golden normalizer. Go (NormalizeXMLForGolden) and TypeScript (normalizeXmlForGolden) both read it, so the canonicalization every XML parity assertion is measured against cannot drift between languages. Each row carries the exact normalized output for both inputs, so the two languages are pinned to the same literal rather than only to the same relation - two implementations returning different strings would otherwise both pass every row. 'equal' restates whether the two outputs coincide; the false rows are the ones that matter, because a normalizer that erases content makes genuinely different documents look identical.

cases.name: entity and literal tab are the same content
cases.why: Go escapes a tab as a character reference where the TypeScript builder emits it literally; absorbing that difference is what this normalizer is for

cases.name: whitespace content is not empty content
cases.why: the collapse used to erase the tab, so these compared equal and a real difference was masked

cases.name: a single space is content too
cases.why: same masking, and space is the shape a serializer is most likely to emit by accident

cases.name: newline content survives in both spellings
cases.why: the content is a newline in both, written two ways

cases.name: a no-break space is content, not formatting
cases.why: U+00A0 is a legal XML character that appears in real tool output. It is in JavaScript's \s but not Go's, so a \s-based collapse erased it in one language only

cases.name: an ideographic space is content, not formatting
cases.why: same class as U+00A0: matched by JavaScript's \s, not Go's

cases.name: a form feed is content, not formatting
cases.why: U+000C is in BOTH languages' \s and in neither encoder, so a \s-based collapse erased it in both — unlike U+00A0 above, which only JavaScript's \s reaches. Pinning both shapes is why the class is XML's S production rather than either language's shorthand

cases.name: indentation between siblings is still collapsed
cases.why: pretty-printing is formatting, not content - collapsing it is the normalizer's original job and must still happen

cases.name: indentation around a nested element is collapsed
cases.why: an open tag followed by another open tag is formatting, not content

cases.name: whitespace after a self-closing element is formatting
cases.why: the discriminating case for the self-closing guard: a self-closing tag opens no element, so what follows it is not content. Drop the guard and this pair diverges

cases.name: a self-closing element is not treated as content
cases.why: the preceding tag ends in '/>', so the whitespace after it is formatting

cases.name: the XML declaration is dropped
cases.why: Go emits a declaration and the TypeScript builder does not

cases.name: apostrophe escapes are equivalent
cases.why: the two libraries pick different escapes for the same character

cases.name: a capital X is not a character reference
cases.why:
XML's CharRef production requires a lowercase x, so 
 is literal text and must not decode. A case-insensitive decoder folded the x in one language and not the other

cases.name: a carriage return decodes in both spellings
cases.why: the CR entry is the one decoder member no other row exercises

cases.name: a byte-order mark is trimmed wherever it sits at a boundary
cases.why: doubled leading and trailing, because a single-leading-BOM strip left both languages disagreeing at the other placements

cases.name: quote escapes are equivalent
cases.why: the double-quote pair, the one decoder entry no other row reaches

cases.name: a lowercase hex digit decodes like an uppercase one
cases.why: Go enumerates the two spellings separately, so each needs its own row; the capital-X row proves only that the x is not folded

cases.name: a lowercase carriage-return reference decodes too
cases.why: the second half of the CR pair

cases.name: a capital X never decodes, for every hex reference
cases.why: the capital-X row covers only the newline reference; a case-insensitive decoder on any of the other three would decode text that XML says is literal

cases.name: a no-break space at the boundary is not trimmed
cases.why: JavaScript's trim() treats NBSP as whitespace and Go's TrimSpace does too, so either shorthand eats it and the boundary stops matching the explicit class. Must be its own row: pairing it with U+0085 lets whichever character a given language does not trim shield the other

cases.name: a next-line character at the boundary is not trimmed
cases.why: the mirror: U+0085 is in Go's TrimSpace but not JavaScript's trim(), so this row pins the Go half of the same invariant

cases.name: literal spaces at the boundary are trimmed
cases.why: the space member of the trim class: dropping it, or adding a form feed, passed every other row

cases.name: a form feed at the boundary is not trimmed
cases.why: form feed is not XML whitespace, so widening the trim class to either language's \s would eat it. Completes the boundary set: space in, form feed and NBSP and U+0085 out
